data.title: MetaOptics Ltd Secures up to S$32 Million Share Subscription Facility from GEM Opportunities Fund ISA Ltd.
data.description:
MetaOptics Ltd Secures up to S$32 Million Share Subscription Facility from GEM Opportunities Fund ISA Ltd.

MetaOptics Ltd Secures up to S$32 Million Share Subscription Facility from GEM Opportunities Fund ISA Ltd.

PR Newswire

SINGAPORE, Nov. 22, 2026

Three-year committed facility provides MetaOptics with flexible growth capital, drawn down at the Company's sole discretion

SINGAPORE, Nov. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MetaOptics Ltd (Catalist: 9MT) (OTCQX: MOTLY) ("MetaOptics" or the "Company", and together with its subsidiaries, the "Group"), a Singapore-headquartered semiconductor optics company pioneering glass-based metalens solutions enhanced by AI-driven image processing, announced that it had on 20 November 2026, entered into a share subscription facility agreement with GEM Opportunities Fund ISA Ltd. ("GEM"), the Bermuda-based investment vehicle managed by Global Emerging Markets (GEM), New York, for an aggregate commitment of up to S$32 million (the "Share Subscription Facility"). The Share Subscription Facility is subject to, inter alia, the approval of the Company's shareholders ("Shareholders") at an extraordinary general meeting ("EGM") to be convened. A circular containing further details of the Share Subscription Facility, together with the notice of EGM, will be despatched to Shareholders in due course.

The Company intends to apply the net proceeds from drawdowns under the Share Subscription Facility, entirely for the Group's working capital purposes, including general corporate expenses, funding the day-to-day operations of the Group and supporting the growth of its existing business. As part of the Group's plans to grow its existing business, the Group intends to establish a new 12-inch glass semiconductor fabrication line in the United States to produce metalenses for co-packaged optics ("CPO") and colour imaging applications. The Share Subscription Facility provides MetaOptics with flexible access to growth capital while allowing the Company to control the timing of any drawdowns, in line with its capital needs and prevailing market conditions.

Mr Thng Chong Kim, Executive Chairman of MetaOptics, said: "This Share Subscription Facility gives us a reliable, flexible source of capital for our day-to-day operations and to support the growth of our existing business by establishing a new 12-inch glass semiconductor fabrication line in the United States, on terms that put MetaOptics in control of the timing and size of each drawdown. We are pleased to have the backing of GEM, an experienced global investor, as we execute on our plans and build long-term value for our Shareholders."

This press release should be read in conjunction with the announcement released by the Company on SGXNet on 23 November 2026 in relation to the Share Subscription Facility.

About MetaOptics Ltd
MetaOptics Ltd (Catalist: 9MT) is a leading-edge semiconductor optics company pioneering glass-based metalens solutions enhanced by AI-driven image processing. Using advanced optical design and a scalable 12-inch DUV lithography process, it powers next-generation applications in CPO, mobile, AR/VR, automotive and other emerging markets. Headquartered in Singapore, MetaOptics aims to deliver high-performance optics with the reliability and scalability demanded by today's most innovative technology brands. Find out more at www.metaoptics.sg.

About GEM
GEM (Global Emerging Markets) is a US$3.4 billion alternative investment group with operations in Paris, New York, Los Angeles and the Bahamas. GEM manages a diverse set of investment vehicles focused on emerging and developed markets and has completed over 600 transactions in 75 countries. Each investment vehicle has a different degree of operational control, risk-adjusted return and liquidity profile. Its family of funds and investment vehicles provides GEM and its partners with exposure to Small-Mid Cap Management Buyouts, Private Investments in Public Equities and select venture investments.  For more information, please visit www.gemny.com.

Forward-Looking Statements
This press release contains forward-looking statements, including statements regarding the share subscription facility, the Company's intended use of proceeds and its business plans. These statements are based on the Company's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. The Facility is subject to shareholder approval at the EGM, and drawdowns under the Facility are subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions and to the execution of definitive documentation. There can be no assurance as to the amount or timing of any funds the Company may ultimately raise. The Company undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements except as required by law.

data.title: Week Ahead for FX, Bonds: Flash PMI Data to Provide Gauge on Economic Growth
data.description:
By Dow Jones Newswires staff

Below are the most important global events likely to affect FX and bond markets in the week starting Nov. 23.

November's flash purchasing managers' surveys for the U.S., eurozone and U.K. will be among the key events. The surveys are an important measure of economic activity and could signal whether there is scope for the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of England to raise interest rates further.

In the U.S, markets will also be closely monitoring Personal Consumption Expenditures price data, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure.

In the Asia-Pacific region, South Korea's interest-rate decision will lead the week, with most analysts expecting a quarter-point increase as strong chip exports fuel growth and inflation remains above target. Inflation data from Australia and Tokyo, along with remarks from a Bank of Japan policy board member, could shape expectations for rate increases in both countries.

China will report October industrial profits as investors watch for Beijing's response to tighter U.S. chip export restrictions.

U.S.

U.S. economic activity and inflation will help investors gauge the path of interest rates in a week shortened by a major holiday.

November's flash manufacturing and services PMI numbers are on tap Monday, as well as a speech by New York Federal Reserve President John Williams at the University of Mount Saint Vincent.

September housing indicators are likely to draw attention Tuesday, as elevated mortgage rates weigh on the sector.

The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index is also scheduled for Tuesday, as consumption continues to be a source of strength for the U.S. economy.

A second estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product growth is due Wednesday. The same day will bring the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures, as consumer prices keep rising faster than the 2% annual pace targeted by the central bank.

"The main message from the report is likely to be that pressure on goods prices is growing," economists at the Investment Institute by UniCredit said in a note. "Overall, October PCE data are likely to keep the Fed firmly on a hiking trajectory."

Durable goods orders, initial jobless claims and new home sales data are also due Wednesday along with the Summary of Commentary on Current Economic Conditions by Federal Reserve District, known as the Beige Book.

Markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving Holiday and will close early on Friday.

U.K.

The U.K. will have a relatively light data release calendar. The November flash estimate purchasing managers' index survey on Monday is the main event.

The U.K. composite PMI, a measure of manufacturing and services activity, rose to 52.9 in October, up from 52.0 in September and the highest reading since February.

"For the November report we imagine that the PMIs ticked higher again," Investec economists said in a note.

Activity might have received a boost from the absence of significant tax increases in the U.K. budget in October as some had feared, they said. U.S. President Trump refraining from renewed large-scale attacks on Iran following the midterm elections might have also helped, not least by helping to lower crude prices, they said. Investec forecasts the composite PMI will rise to 53.1 in November.

Elsewhere, the CBI distributive trades survey is due on Wednesday.

The U.K., meanwhile, plans to sell September 2049 index-linked gilt through syndicated sale, subject to demand and market conditions.

Eurozone

German, French and wider eurozone flash purchasing managers' surveys for November are due on Monday. The eurozone composite purchasing managers index, a measure of manufacturing and services activity, fell to a four-month low of 51.7 in October from 53.1 in September but remained above the 50 level that separates an expansion from a contraction.

"We expect to see some mild weakness in the euro-area PMIs, reflecting the challenging environment for energy markets and tighter financial conditions in Europe," RBC Capital Markets strategists said in a note.

On Tuesday, the German ifo business confidence survey for November will be released. That will be followed by the final third-quarter German gross domestic product report on Wednesday and GfK German consumer confidence survey for December on Thursday.

French and Spanish inflation data for November will be published Friday along with November German labor market data and the European Commission's business confidence survey.

Japan

Bank of Japan policy board member Naoki Tamura will meet with local leaders in the Yamanashi prefecture on Thursday. Investors will watch his remarks for clues on when the central bank might raise rates again.

Tokyo's November consumer-price data are due Friday. The figures are an early indicator of nationwide inflation, and a pickup could strengthen expectations for a rate increase.

BOJ Gov. Kazuo Ueda recently stressed the importance of keeping underlying inflation around the central bank's 2% target. He said inflation excluding fresh food is likely to rise well above 2% as companies pass on higher labor costs, oil prices remain high and the yen stays weak.

The Ministry of Finance will auction about 300 billion yen of 40-year government bonds on Wednesday, reopening an issue first sold in May. The sale could draw demand from insurers and pension funds seeking long-dated debt.

The BOJ is scheduled to buy government bonds in three maturity ranges on Thursday, including those with more than three and up to five years remaining and those with more than 10 and up to 25 years remaining.

Japanese markets will be closed Monday for a national holiday.

China

A thin data slate awaits in China. The sole release of note drops Friday, which will show how China's industrial firms fared in October.

Economists will look at the figures to see if industrial profit growth held up last month after surging in September. Spending tied to artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure has been a key driver of profits over the year, though that hasn't benefited all sectors evenly.

Focus will also be on any potential announcements from Beijing after Xi Jinping's meetings with Trump didn't yield much in the way of progress on key trade and geopolitical issues. Markets will be watching ministry statements closely after Chinese officials warned of potential countermeasures to U.S. moves to tighten chip-export restrictions.

Australia / New Zealand

Australia's October inflation report on Wednesday will help shape expectations for the Reserve Bank of Australia's December rate decision. In September, annual headline inflation rose to 4.3% and trimmed-mean inflation climbed to 3.6%.

Third-quarter capital spending data due Thursday will show how much businesses invested and whether they revised their spending plans. The RBA will publish its bulletin the same day.

In New Zealand, third-quarter retail sales data due Monday will show how household spending is holding up ahead of the central bank's Dec. 9 rate decision.

South Korea

Bank of Korea is expected to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter-percentage-point to 3.25% on Thursday after leaving it unchanged in October.

Some analysts also expect the bank to raise its growth and inflation forecasts for 2026 and 2027 as demand for chips used in artificial intelligence boosts exports and price pressures persist.

The central bank signaled it would raise its growth forecasts after third-quarter gross domestic product grew faster than expected. It expects inflation to stay above its 2% target through 2027.

The International Monetary Fund, the Korea Development Institute and Citi Research raised their growth forecasts for South Korea earlier this month, citing strength in the semiconductor industry.

Singapore

Singapore's consumer-price index likely rose 1.9% in October from a year earlier, down from 2.2% in September, according to the median estimate of six economists polled by The Wall Street Journal. Core inflation, which excludes private road transport and accommodation costs, likely slowed to 1.6% from 2.0%, the poll showed. The data are due Monday.

Lower fourth-quarter electricity tariffs and a high year-earlier comparison likely helped ease inflation, said UOB economist Jester Koh.

Final third-quarter gross domestic product figures are due Tuesday. An advance estimate showed the economy grew 5.4% from a year earlier. DBS economists expect that figure to be revised up to 5.6%, mainly because manufacturing grew faster than initially reported.

DBS expects the government to forecast growth of 2.5% to 4.5% for 2027.

Any references to days are in local times.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

data.title: Australia Business Conditions Contract at Fastest Pace in 5 Years
data.description:
By James Glynn

SYDNEY--Australian business conditions contracted at their fastest pace in five years in November, adding to concerns that the economy has slowed sharply following five interest rate rises since the start of 2026.

The headline seasonally adjusted S&P Global Flash Australia PMI composite output index remained below the 50.0 neutral mark for a second consecutive month in November. At 46.1--down from 48.2--the reading was the lowest since August 2021.

The decline was attributed to deeper contractions in output across both the manufacturing and service sectors, with the rates of decline the strongest in 25 and 36 months, respectively.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised interest rates aggressively in response to elevated inflation. The official cash rate now stands at 4.85%, its highest level in 18 years.

"November's flash PMI data revealed that Australia's business conditions deteriorated at the sharpest pace in more than five years as the reduction in new orders turned broad-based, with services new business now also in contraction," said Jingyi Pan, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The PMI data followed last week's release of data showing unemployment jumped in October to 4.9%. Economists expect the RBA to hold rates at its next policy meeting in December.

"The latest decline in demand reflected the impact of higher interest rates, while softening domestic and external conditions also contributed," Pan said.

Inflationary pressures eased for the first time in several months as demand softened across the board, speaking to the effectiveness of the recent tightening of financial conditions, she added.

The data also showed employment fell alongside a marked reduction in business confidence among private-sector firms, pointing to more subdued near-term output conditions at a time when inflation has yet to be fully brought under control, Pan said.

-Write to James Glynn at james.glynn@wsj.com

data.title: Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners Announces Sale of StraitNZ
data.description:
Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners Announces Sale of StraitNZ

Morgan Stanley Investment Management (MSIM), through investment funds managed by Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners (MSIP), its private infrastructure investment platform, today announced it has entered into an agreement to sell StraitNZ (the Company), a New Zealand-based integrated transport, logistics and ferry company, to Partners Group, a leading global private markets firm, acting on behalf of its clients.

StraitNZ manages multiple daily freight and passenger services across the Cook Strait in New Zealand. StraitNZ is one of only two Cook Strait ferry operators, connecting New Zealand’s national highway system from the North Island to the South Island. Since MSIP’s investment in March 2022, the Company completed a full fleet refresh, introduced three-year CPI-linked take-or-pay freight contracts, rolled out dynamic passenger pricing, secured multi-decade port lease extensions and delivered strong EBITDA growth.

“StraitNZ demonstrates MSIP’s ability to identify high-quality essential infrastructure businesses and create value through active ownership and disciplined execution,” said Mark McLean, Managing Director and Co-Head of Asia-Pacific investing for MSIP. “Over our ownership period, we have worked alongside management to strengthen the Company’s commercial proposition, improve operational performance and position StraitNZ for sustainable long-term growth.”

Through its ferries and nationwide road freight network, StraitNZ provides an essential freight and passenger link, connecting customers, communities and businesses across New Zealand’s supply chain. Services are expected to continue as normal while the transaction is completed.

The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals and other closing conditions.

About Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners
Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners (MSIP) is a leading global private infrastructure investment platform with approximately $17 billion in capital commitments since inception. Founded in 2006, MSIP has invested in a diverse portfolio across transportation, digital, energy transition, and water and waste. MSIP targets assets that provide essential public goods and services with the potential for value creation through active ownership. For further information about Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners, please visit Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners.

Morgan Stanley Investment Management
Morgan Stanley Investment Management, together with its investment advisory affiliates, has more than 1,300 investment professionals around the world and $2.1 trillion in assets under management or supervision as of September 30, 2026. Morgan Stanley Investment Management strives to provide outstanding long-term investment performance, service, and a comprehensive suite of investment management solutions to a diverse client base, which includes governments, institutions, corporations and individuals worldwide. For further information about Morgan Stanley Investment Management, please visit www.morganstanley.com/im.

Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS) is a leading global financial services firm providing a wide range of investment banking, securities, wealth management and investment management services. With offices in 42 countries, the Firm’s employees serve clients worldwide including corporations, governments, institutions and individuals. data.title: Corporate America hunts for 'generational' growth in AI, trading cards and the L.A. airport
data.description:
By Bill Peters

There's been no shortage of trends deemed once-in-a-generation by executives on earnings calls

Delta recently praised "generational airport investments" in Los Angeles.

On earnings calls over recent weeks, there's been very little that executives couldn't spin into a "generational" opportunity.

The adjective has come up on numerous calls. Executives have naturally cast artificial intelligence as a "generational" shift. But they've also described a boom in trading cards and flights to Fort Lauderdale, Fla., as "generational." Renovations at Los Angeles International Airport? Also, apparently, "generational."

For instance, Morgan Stanley (MS), during its earnings call last month, said the bank was helping clients stay on top of AI, be it through innovation or matters related to spending on the technology.

"We all see that the power of AI as an efficiency and productivity and resiliency tool is [an] incontrovertible, generational jump in technology," CEO Ted Pick said.

Elsewhere, the investment firm Blackstone (BX) said it had become a crucial provider of capital in the AI landscape, adding that its data-center portfolio rested on solid, long-term contracts with "highly creditworthy counterparties."

"As the AI revolution progresses, the rising demand for capital is creating generational opportunities for those with the platform, relationships, capabilities and discipline to meet this demand," CEO Stephen Schwarzman said on the company's earnings call last month.

Blackrock (BLK), another investment firm, said on its call last month that companies "need to fund a generational AI buildout," and that the firm was at the center of many conversations related to that buildout. And fintech company Fiserv (FISV) said this month that AI had spurred "a generational transformation" in software development.

That generational talk has run up against deeper pressures on the AI trade - which has lately been dogged by concerns over Big Tech's epic spending and borrowing plans to develop the technology, the ouster of Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang and the reality of a Democrat-controlled Congress next year. More broadly, consumers are still navigating higher prices.

Big Tech, and in turn artificial intelligence, have done much of the work to prop up the S&P 500 index SPX over the past few years. However, according to a FactSet report released Friday, the so-called Magnificent Seven tech companies - Apple (AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG), Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META), Nvidia and Tesla (TSLA) - reported lower earnings growth than the rest of the index for the third quarter. The S&P 500 is down around 10% over the past month.

Still, "generational" shifts are happening elsewhere. For Hasbro (HAS), which owns the fantasy card game Magic: The Gathering, that shift was happening in trading cards. Sales of the game have hit record levels, as Hasbro leans on rarities and a collectible market for cards that some are increasingly treating like an investment.

"I think trading cards over the last year have emerged as the No. 1 category in toys and games," Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks said in October. "I think they're actually bigger than building blocks now, and we see that as a generational structural shift and not just as kind of, like, a one-time thing."

In October, Boeing (BA) said it had "scored a generational win" with the U.S. Navy, which chose it to build a fighter jet. Kimberly-Clark (KMB) - known for brands like Huggies and Kleenex - described its acquisition of Kenvue this month as a "generational opportunity" to meet consumers' increasingly personalized health and wellness needs.

JetBlue Airways (JBLU) last month described expanded flight service to Fort Lauderdale as a "generational opportunity for us." Even Los Angeles International Airport - long considered a traffic and infrastructure nightmare - got a shout-out from Delta Air Lines (DAL), which has invested money to renovate and connect terminals and expand its lounges at the airport.

Delta's chief commercial officer, Joe Esposito, said on the airline's earnings call last month that it was adding service from Los Angeles to the South Pacific, Hong Kong and Manila, Philippines.

"This has been enabled by generational airport investments at L.A. to create a modern, connected complex with additional gate capacity and seamless access to the international terminal," Esposito said.

-Bill Peters

data.title: Ron Johnson's Social Security gaffe buried important news
data.description:
By Brett Arends

Wisconsin Republican's remarks overshadowed what might have been a useful Senate committee hearing about fixing Social Security

Sen. Ron Johnson's gaffe about shutting down Social Security drowned out the latest Senate deliberations on the subject.

Spare a thought for Ron Johnson.

The Republican senator from Wisconsin is suffering from "Long Ayn Rand." He was exposed to the famous author's radical right-wing ideas when he was younger, and sadly he's never recovered.

Johnson, who called Rand's tedious, doorstopping allegory "Atlas Shrugged" his "foundational book," just suffered a serious Long Ayn Rand relapse live on TV. It caused him to stick both feet in his mouth and denounce Social Security as a "Ponzi" scheme that should be "shut down."

Many people catch Ayn Rand disease (or the left-wing version, Karl Marx disease) when they are young. Most grow out of it by their early 20s. A few, tragically, have the chronic condition for life. There is no cure.

(Among others tragically affected by Long Ayn Rand was the novelist's friend, the late Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, whose condition led him to a series of spectacular blunders.)

It was a shame that Johnson suffered his LAR relapse on TV because it overshadowed what might otherwise have been a useful Senate committee hearing about how to fix, or rescue, Social Security. Democratic committee colleagues of Johnson's spent most of a 90-minute hearing on Social Security quoting the Republican's gaffe in various tones of fury and disbelief. Johnson repeatedly had to argue that he had misspoken, or spoken poorly, and that he didn't want to shut down Social Security. He said that he was proposing a bill to make sure benefits are never cut, no matter what happens to the trust fund.

It was all pointless.

It is not my job to defend or explain U.S. senators when they say or do stupid things in public. But buried under Johnson's gaffe were some useful points that ought to be widely understood - no matter where you are politically. They are essential to understanding the crisis facing Social Security, and any proposals to shore up its finances.

The first is that almost nobody - including Johnson - is proposing cutting Social Security benefits from current levels. The most conservative, right-wing proposals being put forward consist of scaling back future benefit increases so that they are only in line with inflation. So someone retiring in 20 or 30 years would get the same benefit - in constant dollars - as someone retiring today. (These are proposals to avoid the current situation, which would cause deep, automatic cuts in six or eight years' time. Everyone admits this would be a disaster, and everyone wants to avoid it.)

This is exactly the idea recently put forward by John Cogan, a fellow at Stanford University's conservative Hoover Institution. He proposes limiting the growth of average Social Security benefits per person to match economywide inflation, and calls for the growth of Medicare and other federal medical benefits to match specific healthcare inflation.

"Limiting the growth in cash entitlement benefits per recipient to consumer price inflation and the growth in healthcare entitlement spending per recipient to the growth in economywide healthcare costs would restrain the growth in federal spending to 2.9 percent per year," he writes. "The spending limitation would reduce the budget deficit by two-thirds in 15 years and balance the budget in 20 years," he adds.

To be clear, I am neither endorsing (nor critiquing) Cogan's proposal. And you can certainly challenge some of his mathematical and economic assumptions. But the general point is important: Among responsible or respected analysts, even the very conservative are not talking seriously about cutting Social Security benefits from today's levels. And, maybe more important, the expected costs of future benefits growth are so big that simply freezing benefits in real terms - in other words, raising them no more than inflation in future years - can have a huge impact on the budget math.

Would this be a "cut?" Yes and no. On one level, obviously, keeping benefits the same in real terms is not a cut compared with today. But it would be a cut compared with what is currently projected.

It is little understood, but Social Security contains a built-in escalator that gives every cohort of retirees per year, even adjusted for inflation, more than their predecessors. This is in addition to the annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, which all beneficiaries receive every year. It applies to your initial benefits and is based on something called "average wage indexing." It was introduced in the 1970s. It means every cohort gets a raise compared with the one before. But if we give every new retiree more than predecessors, while the number of retirees is also ballooning, and retirees are living much longer than before, that raises obvious mathematical issues.

Johnson's other reasonable point is that the so-called Social Security trust fund is a fiction. There is no fund. There is no lockbox. The so-called assets owned by the fund are simply accounting entries, whereby the federal government promises to pay future benefits out of general taxation or borrowing. So retirees aren't "getting their own money back." Their Social Security payroll taxes went to pay the benefits of their parents' and grandparents' generations. When they retire, their benefits will be paid by their children and grandchildren.

The thing about Social Security reform that everyone should remember is that multiple things are true at the same time. Many of the Democratic talking points are perfectly true. So are many of the Republican talking points. It's often not either-or. It's and ... and ... and ...

The best comment of the day came from Virginia Democrat Mark Warner. He pointed out that fixing Social Security was really just a question of math: raising program revenues and slowing the growth of future costs. "To say we can't fix this is outrageous," he said. "It is eminently fixable. This is math. It isn't policy changes. It's math."

Quite so.

-Brett Arends

data.title: Week Ahead for FX, Bonds: Flash PMI Data to Provide Gauge on Economic Growth
data.description:
By Dow Jones Newswires staff

Below are the most important global events likely to affect FX and bond markets in the week starting Nov. 23.

November's flash purchasing managers' surveys for the U.S., eurozone and U.K. will be among the key events. The surveys are an important measure of economic activity and could signal whether there is scope for the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of England to raise interest rates further.

In the U.S, markets will also be closely monitoring Personal Consumption Expenditures price data, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure.

In the Asia-Pacific region, South Korea's interest-rate decision will lead the week, with most analysts expecting a quarter-point increase as strong chip exports fuel growth and inflation remains above target. Inflation data from Australia and Tokyo, along with remarks from a Bank of Japan policy board member, could shape expectations for rate increases in both countries.

China will report October industrial profits as investors watch for Beijing's response to tighter U.S. chip export restrictions.

U.S.

U.S. economic activity and inflation will help investors gauge the path of interest rates in a week shortened by a major holiday.

November's flash manufacturing and services PMI numbers are on tap Monday, as well as a speech by New York Federal Reserve President John Williams at the University of Mount Saint Vincent.

September housing indicators are likely to draw attention Tuesday, as elevated mortgage rates weigh on the sector.

The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index is also scheduled for Tuesday, as consumption continues to be a source of strength for the U.S. economy.

A second estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product growth is due Wednesday. The same day will bring the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures, as consumer prices keep rising faster than the 2% annual pace targeted by the central bank.

"The main message from the report is likely to be that pressure on goods prices is growing," economists at the Investment Institute by UniCredit said in a note. "Overall, October PCE data are likely to keep the Fed firmly on a hiking trajectory."

Durable goods orders, initial jobless claims and new home sales data are also due Wednesday along with the Summary of Commentary on Current Economic Conditions by Federal Reserve District, known as the Beige Book.

Markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving Holiday and will close early on Friday.

U.K.

The U.K. will have a relatively light data release calendar. The November flash estimate purchasing managers' index survey on Monday is the main event.

The U.K. composite PMI, a measure of manufacturing and services activity, rose to 52.9 in October, up from 52.0 in September and the highest reading since February.

"For the November report we imagine that the PMIs ticked higher again," Investec economists said in a note.

Activity might have received a boost from the absence of significant tax increases in the U.K. budget in October as some had feared, they said. U.S. President Trump refraining from renewed large-scale attacks on Iran following the midterm elections might have also helped, not least by helping to lower crude prices, they said. Investec forecasts the composite PMI will rise to 53.1 in November.

Elsewhere, the CBI distributive trades survey is due on Wednesday.

The U.K., meanwhile, plans to sell September 2049 index-linked gilt through syndicated sale, subject to demand and market conditions.

Eurozone

German, French and wider eurozone flash purchasing managers' surveys for November are due on Monday. The eurozone composite purchasing managers index, a measure of manufacturing and services activity, fell to a four-month low of 51.7 in October from 53.1 in September but remained above the 50 level that separates an expansion from a contraction.

"We expect to see some mild weakness in the euro-area PMIs, reflecting the challenging environment for energy markets and tighter financial conditions in Europe," RBC Capital Markets strategists said in a note.

On Tuesday, the German ifo business confidence survey for November will be released. That will be followed by the final third-quarter German gross domestic product report on Wednesday and GfK German consumer confidence survey for December on Thursday.

French and Spanish inflation data for November will be published Friday along with November German labor market data and the European Commission's business confidence survey.

Japan

Bank of Japan policy board member Naoki Tamura will meet with local leaders in the Yamanashi prefecture on Thursday. Investors will watch his remarks for clues on when the central bank might raise rates again.

Tokyo's November consumer-price data are due Friday. The figures are an early indicator of nationwide inflation, and a pickup could strengthen expectations for a rate increase.

BOJ Gov. Kazuo Ueda recently stressed the importance of keeping underlying inflation around the central bank's 2% target. He said inflation excluding fresh food is likely to rise well above 2% as companies pass on higher labor costs, oil prices remain high and the yen stays weak.

The Ministry of Finance will auction about 300 billion yen of 40-year government bonds on Wednesday, reopening an issue first sold in May. The sale could draw demand from insurers and pension funds seeking long-dated debt.

The BOJ is scheduled to buy government bonds in three maturity ranges on Thursday, including those with more than three and up to five years remaining and those with more than 10 and up to 25 years remaining.

Japanese markets will be closed Monday for a national holiday.

China

A thin data slate awaits in China. The sole release of note drops Friday, which will show how China's industrial firms fared in October.

Economists will look at the figures to see if industrial profit growth held up last month after surging in September. Spending tied to artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure has been a key driver of profits over the year, though that hasn't benefited all sectors evenly.

Focus will also be on any potential announcements from Beijing after Xi Jinping's meetings with Trump didn't yield much in the way of progress on key trade and geopolitical issues. Markets will be watching ministry statements closely after Chinese officials warned of potential countermeasures to U.S. moves to tighten chip-export restrictions.

Australia / New Zealand

Australia's October inflation report on Wednesday will help shape expectations for the Reserve Bank of Australia's December rate decision. In September, annual headline inflation rose to 4.3% and trimmed-mean inflation climbed to 3.6%.

Third-quarter capital spending data due Thursday will show how much businesses invested and whether they revised their spending plans. The RBA will publish its bulletin the same day.

In New Zealand, third-quarter retail sales data due Monday will show how household spending is holding up ahead of the central bank's Dec. 9 rate decision.

South Korea

Bank of Korea is expected to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter-percentage-point to 3.25% on Thursday after leaving it unchanged in October.

Some analysts also expect the bank to raise its growth and inflation forecasts for 2026 and 2027 as demand for chips used in artificial intelligence boosts exports and price pressures persist.

The central bank signaled it would raise its growth forecasts after third-quarter gross domestic product grew faster than expected. It expects inflation to stay above its 2% target through 2027.

The International Monetary Fund, the Korea Development Institute and Citi Research raised their growth forecasts for South Korea earlier this month, citing strength in the semiconductor industry.

Singapore

Singapore's consumer-price index likely rose 1.9% in October from a year earlier, down from 2.2% in September, according to the median estimate of six economists polled by The Wall Street Journal. Core inflation, which excludes private road transport and accommodation costs, likely slowed to 1.6% from 2.0%, the poll showed. The data are due Monday.

Lower fourth-quarter electricity tariffs and a high year-earlier comparison likely helped ease inflation, said UOB economist Jester Koh.

Final third-quarter gross domestic product figures are due Tuesday. An advance estimate showed the economy grew 5.4% from a year earlier. DBS economists expect that figure to be revised up to 5.6%, mainly because manufacturing grew faster than initially reported.

DBS expects the government to forecast growth of 2.5% to 4.5% for 2027.

Any references to days are in local times.
